unit.title: The digestive system
unit.blurb: The amazing journey of food through your body, your teeth, and how to eat a balanced diet.

O1.t: Name the parts of the digestive system and describe what each part does.

O2.t: Describe the jobs of incisors, canines and molars, and how to look after teeth.

O3.t: Describe a balanced diet and what carbohydrates, proteins, vitamins, minerals and fibre do.

O4.t: Use a food diary to judge whether a diet is balanced and suggest healthy swaps.

captions: Hello, body explorers! Is anyone hungry? Me too!
This is lesson 4.1: parts of the digestive system.
You take a big bite of a sandwich. Mmm!
Then it goes on an amazing journey through a tube about nine metres long. That is as long as a bus!
Along the way, your body breaks the food down and takes out the goodness, called nutrients. This is digestion.
And whatever is left over comes out as waste. Yes, poo!
Digestion starts in the mouth, where teeth chop the food and saliva makes it soft and slippery.
You swallow, and the food slides down the oesophagus, a stretchy tube.
In the stomach, strong muscles churn the food with acid, like a washing machine.
In the small intestine, nutrients pass into the blood.
Then the large intestine takes back water, and the waste leaves the body.
Pause and think. Where do nutrients pass into the blood?
Your teeth have different jobs. Incisors at the front are sharp, for cutting and biting.
Pointy canines grip and tear food.
And big, flat molars at the back grind and chew. Brush them twice a day to keep them healthy!
Did you know? An empty stomach is about the size of your fist.
But it is so stretchy that it can hold about one and a half litres after a big meal!
Have you ever heard your tummy gurgle in a quiet classroom? Oops!
It is just gas and liquid being squeezed along your intestines.
It is completely normal. Your digestive system is busy working!
Your turn. Which teeth grind and chew food?
Let's make a messy model of digestion.
Put some crackers and a little water in a zip bag, and squash them. This is like the stomach.
Then pour the mush into an old stocking, and squeeze it along. This is like the intestines.
The liquid seeping out is like nutrients passing into the blood. What is left is the waste!
Let's remember.
Digestion breaks food down into nutrients.
Food travels from the mouth, down the oesophagus, to the stomach, then the intestines.
Nutrients pass into the blood in the small intestine.
And incisors cut, canines tear, and molars grind.
Tummy-tastic work! Now go to the practice room and say the new words.

captions: Hello, healthy eaters! What did you have for breakfast?
This is lesson 4.2: balanced diets.
A balanced diet means eating the right amounts of different kinds of food.
Imagine your plate. About a third should be fruit and vegetables, and about a third should be carbohydrates, like rice, bread and pasta, for energy.
Add some protein for growing, some dairy for strong bones, and just a little fat and sugar.
Pause and think. Which food group gives us lots of energy?
Carbohydrates give us energy to run, jump and think.
Proteins, in meat, fish, eggs and beans, help us grow and repair our bodies.
Vitamins and minerals, in fruit and vegetables, keep us healthy. Carrots even help your eyes!
And fibre keeps food moving through your intestines.
Sam's lunch is chips and doughnuts. Tasty, but lots of fat and sugar.
By the afternoon, Sam feels tired and grumpy.
Let's give it a makeover. Swap the doughnut for an apple, and add a salad and a chicken wrap.
Now Sam has a balanced lunch, with energy that lasts all afternoon!
Did you know? Your body is about sixty percent water.
So drinking water every day is an important part of a healthy diet.
Joke time! Why did the banana go to the doctor?
Because it wasn't peeling well!
Your turn. Why do we need protein?
Let's keep a food diary.
Write down everything you eat and drink for one whole day.
Sort each food into its group, and count your portions of fruit and vegetables.
Is your diet balanced? What is one healthy swap you could make?
Let's remember.
A balanced diet has the right amounts of each food group.
Carbohydrates give us energy.
Proteins help us grow and repair our bodies.
And vitamins, minerals and fibre keep us healthy.
Delicious work! Now go to the practice room and say the new words.
